blocks.content: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter its basic structure or framework.

rows: Only the unconstitutional part of a law is declared void, provided it is separable.
Inconsistent pre-constitutional laws remain dormant rather than completely void.
Examines the true nature of a statute to resolve legislative jurisdiction overlaps.
Prevents legislature from indirectly breaching constitutional limits on legislative power.

items: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) is frequently tested as the origin of the Doctrine of Basic Structure.
Competitive exams regularly contrast the Doctrine of Severability with the Doctrine of Eclipse under Article 13.
Questions on Seventh Schedule competence frequently focus on the Doctrine of Pith and Substance and Colorable Legislation.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Doctrine of Basic Structure was established in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) to limit Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368.
The Doctrine of Severability (Article 13) provides that only the unconstitutional portion of a statute is declared void, leaving the remaining valid portion intact if separable.
The Doctrine of Eclipse holds that pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights become dormant rather than dead, and can be revived by constitutional amendment.
The Doctrine of Pith and Substance determines the true nature and character of legislation to decide legislative competence when list jurisdictions overlap.
The Doctrine of Colorable Legislation prevents the legislature from indirectly exceeding its constitutional limits when it lacks direct power to enact a law.
